Occurrences.Kwic: 其僧一似韓獹逐塊。連忙上階。捉其月影相似。又問。如何是無寒暑處。山云。寒時寒殺闍黎。熱時熱殺闍黎。如韓獹逐塊走到階上。又却不見月影。韓獹乃出戰國策。云韓氏之獹駿狗也。中山之兔狡兔也。是其獹方能尋其兔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Blue Cliff Record of Chan Master Foguo Yuanwu (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄). Yuanwu Keqin compares the unnamed monk to the Han hound chasing a reflected moon and then explains the hound-and-rabbit allusion from the Strategies of the Warring States.

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: A Blue Cliff Record comment gives the named allusion: the hound of the Han family was a swift dog, capable of tracking the cunning hare of Zhongshan; Yuanwu Keqin compares the unnamed monk in Dongshan's cold-and-heat exchange to that hound running up the steps after a reflected moon and finding no moon there.
EvidenceBody: Across the corpus the compact phrase is repeatedly contrasted with "the lion bites the person" (師子咬人，韓獹逐塊): one address says, "you must have the lion bite the person; do not imitate the Han hound chasing the clod" (直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊). It also occurs as a verdict after answers in public exchanges and as a verse line on Zhaozhou's attendant case. Zen bends the old hunting-dog allusion into a stock contrast between the person and the thrown clod, but the entry goes no farther than the corpus's own lion/person and hound/clod pairing.
